findings.text: Within the first paragraph a newcomer learns what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. This answers the "what is it" and "why does it matter" questions quickly.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The next step is linked from the top of the page, so a newcomer does not have to scroll through the long study to find out what to do.
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" linking to #next-steps

findings.text: The install path is concrete: prerequisites, clone, setup script and a first command. It does not say whether a Claude account or API key is needed, or where to run the command (which repository and directory).
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" ... "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: Someone arriving at Athena's home URL gets a long technical study of a different project, firstmate. The second paragraph explains why, but nearly the whole page is about firstmate, not Athena.
findings.source: Title: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"; lede: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project"

findings.text: The page never shows Athena's main promise in action: no example request, commit, cost record or verdict appears. What the study does show is the traceability of its claims, a different feature from the one the lede advertises.
findings.source: Lede: "records what each step cost" and "get back a commit they can trace to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict"

findings.text: A newcomer has no context for this link: whose proposals, and why would a visitor decide anything? It reads like an internal control on a public page.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The body is dense with firstmate jargon: captain, yolo, secondmate, places-held, exit 75. A newcomer to Athena will skim it rather than learn from it, though the definitions and claim links make it checkable.
findings.source: Transitions cards, e.g. t8: "a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none, and a secondmate with no endpoint is recovered by the spawn script instead"

findings.text: Terms are defined before they are used, which helps. The duplicate definitions add length, though, and the glossary is long.
findings.source: Start here "Words used first" and the Glossary: "Each is defined here, and again in the Glossary at the end of the page."

findings.text: Saying what the study did not check is honest and fits the traceability pitch. But telling a first-time visitor that the first reading missed several paths may lower their confidence in what Athena can do.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths"
